learn.concept: A security attack is any action that threatens confidentiality, integrity, or availability of information or systems. Textbooks split attacks into passive (observe without changing resources) and active (alter data, processes, or availability). Exam stems usually ask you to classify the behaviour first, then map it to CIA.
learn.howItWorks:
Passive attacks
- Goal: learn what is being sent or who talks to whom.
- Release of message contents: read email, files, calls.
- Traffic analysis: even with encryption, timing, length, and endpoints leak patterns.
- Hard to detect (nothing is changed); prevention (encryption, traffic padding) matters more.

Active attacks
- Masquerade: pretend to be another entity.
- Replay: capture then resend to produce an unauthorised effect.
- Modification: change, delay, or reorder messages.
- Denial of service: block or overload a service.

CIA asset view
- Interception → confidentiality.
- Modification / fabrication → integrity.
- Interruption → availability.
learn.example: **Scenario:** An adversary records only the lengths and times of encrypted VPN sessions between two offices and never changes a packet. That is **traffic analysis** — still passive. If they later replay a captured login token, the attack becomes **active**.

compare.title: Passive
bullets: Hard to detect; focus on prevention

remember: “Only listening / sniffing” → passive; “altering packets” → active.
Traffic analysis is passive even when no plaintext is recovered.
DoS / crash service → interruption (availability), not interception.
Fabrication inserts a fake object; modification changes an existing one.
Masquerade and replay are active authenticity/integrity threats.

bullets: Passive = observe; active = alter or disrupt.
Masquerade, replay, modification, DoS are the classic active set.
Prevention for passive; detection + recovery for active.

flash.q: Passive vs active in one line?
flash.a: Passive learns without changing resources; active changes data, process, or availability.

flash.q: Is traffic analysis passive or active?
flash.a: Passive — patterns are observed; resources are not altered.
Availability (asset destroyed, blocked, or overloaded).

flash.q: Replay of a captured auth message?
flash.a: Active attack (unauthorised effect from re-sending).

commonConfusion.title: Common confusion
commonConfusion.body: **Traffic analysis feels invasive — it is still passive.**\nPassive = observe without changing resources. Active = alter, fabricate, replay, or interrupt.

learn.concept: A security service is the protection goal you want (confidentiality, integrity, authentication, non-repudiation, access control, availability). A security mechanism is the concrete process or device that detects, prevents, or recovers from attacks. Exam questions almost always test this what-versus-how split.
learn.howItWorks:
Core message/entity services
- Confidentiality: only intended parties can read the content (typically via encipherment).
- Integrity: data arrives unaltered; often supported by checksums/MACs.
- Authentication: prove the claimed sender or user identity.
- Non-repudiation: a party cannot later deny a prior action; usually needs signatures/TTP.
- Entity authentication: verify the user before granting service access.

Example mechanisms from the SLM
- Encipherment, access control, notarization, data integrity checks,
  authentication exchange, digital signatures.

Mapping rule
- One mechanism can support several services (encryption aids secrecy and can feed integrity).
- One service may need several mechanisms (non-repudiation needs more than a plain MAC).
learn.example:
**Scenario:** Fahad sends payroll data to a company server.
- Nobody else should read it → **confidentiality** (mechanism: encryption).
- Server must detect modification → **integrity** (mechanism: MAC / hash with protection).
- Server must verify who sent it → **authentication** (credentials or signatures).
Exam habit: name the *service* first, then a plausible *mechanism*.

compare.title: Security service
bullets: Exam cue: not an algorithm name

compare.title: Security mechanism
bullets: Examples: cipher, MAC, signature, firewall, PIN
Exam cue: tool or process, not CIA label alone

remember: Service = goal; mechanism = technique.
Stem asks for a service → confidentiality/authentication/… not “AES”.
Stem asks for a mechanism → cipher, hash, signature, firewall, etc.
Authentication ≠ authorisation (identity proof vs permission).
Non-repudiation usually needs signatures or a trusted third party — not only a MAC.

bullets: Services name protection goals; mechanisms implement them.
Confidentiality ↔ encipherment is the classic pairing.
Integrity often uses appended check values; authentication proves origin.
Non-repudiation is stronger than “I have the message”.
One-to-many mapping both ways between services and mechanisms.

flash.a: Service = security goal; mechanism = process/device that achieves it.
Confidentiality, integrity, authentication, non-repudiation.

flash.q: Is encryption a service or a mechanism?
flash.a: Mechanism (encipherment) that mainly supports confidentiality.

flash.q: Why is a MAC alone weak for non-repudiation?
flash.a: Both parties share the key; either could have made the tag.

commonConfusion.title: Authentication ≠ authorisation
commonConfusion.body: **Authentication** asks *who are you?*\n**Authorisation** asks *what are you allowed to do?*\nA service name is a goal (confidentiality); encryption is a mechanism, not a service.

learn.concept: Classical encryption covers pre-computer and early electromechanical schemes built mainly from substitution and transposition under a shared secret key. Know the five ingredients of a symmetric model: plaintext, encryption algorithm, secret key, ciphertext, decryption algorithm. Modern practice assumes Kerckhoffs: algorithm public, key secret.
learn.howItWorks:
Symmetric model
- Y = E(K, X); X = D(K, Y).
- Same key must reach sender and receiver securely and stay secret.
- Adversary is assumed to know E and D and to observe Y.

Two classical families
- Substitution: replace symbols (Caesar, Playfair, Vigenère).
- Transposition: reorder positions (rail fence, columnar).
- Product ciphers stack stages (later rotor machines / modern rounds).

Security requirements (from the SLM)
- Strong algorithm: ciphertext alone (or with known plaintext) should not yield key/plaintext.
- Secure key distribution and storage — key compromise opens all traffic under that key.
- Brute force: try keys until plaintext looks meaningful (~half the key space on average).
learn.example: Exam habit: first name plaintext/ciphertext/key, then say whether the stem describes replacement (substitution) or reordering (transposition). Do not shrink “classical” to only Caesar.
remember: Classical crypto ≈ substitution + transposition under a shared key.
Cryptography designs schemes; cryptanalysis breaks or stress-tests them.
Kerckhoffs: assume the adversary knows the algorithm.
Secure use needs a strong algorithm and a protected secret key.
Caesar is one substitution instance — not the whole topic.

bullets: Five ingredients: plaintext, algorithm, key, ciphertext, decryption.
Y=E(K,X), X=D(K,Y) under a shared K.
Substitution vs transposition is the first branching question.
Brute force needs a way to recognise valid plaintext.

flash.a: Original message vs encoded/encrypted form.

flash.q: What must be secret in a modern cipher?
flash.a: The key (algorithm is assumed public).
Transposition cipher.
Design of ciphers vs attacking/analysing them.

learn.concept: A substitution cipher replaces plaintext units with ciphertext units by a mapping. Monoalphabetic schemes use one fixed alphabet for the whole message; polyalphabetic schemes change alphabets with position (Vigenère). Classic syllabus set: Caesar, Playfair, polyalphabetic/Vigenère, and the one-time pad idea.
learn.howItWorks:
Caesar / shift
- C = (p + k) mod 26; P = (C − k) mod 26; nontrivial k ∈ 1..25.
- Tiny key space → trivial brute force; frequencies unchanged.

Playfair
- Digraph cipher on a 5×5 keyword square (I/J shared).
- Rules: same row → right neighbour; same column → below; else rectangle corners.
- Stronger than simple letter substitution (676 digraphs vs 26 letters).

Polyalphabetic / Vigenère
- Repeating keyword selects which Caesar shift applies at each position.
- Flattens single-letter frequencies; still breakable (Kasiski / Friedman).

One-time pad
- Random keystream as long as the message, used once, XOR (or mod-26).
- Information-theoretically strong if key is truly random and never reused; impractical at scale.
learn.example: Caesar with k=3: “pay more money” → “SDB PRUH PRQHB”. For Vigenère, align a repeating keyword under the plaintext and look up each (key letter, plaintext letter) pair.

compare.title: Monoalphabetic
bullets: One mapping for the whole message

remember: Stem “shift by 3 / ROT” → Caesar.
Stem “one mapping for all letters” → monoalphabetic.
Playfair works on pairs (digraphs), not single letters.
Polyalphabetic ≠ unbreakable — Kasiski still applies.
OTP security collapses if the keystream is reused.

bullets: Substitution replaces symbols by a keyed mapping.
Caesar: C=(p+k) mod 26; only 25 nontrivial keys.
Playfair: 5×5 digraph cipher; stronger frequency profile.
Vigenère: repeating keyword of Caesar shifts.
OTP: perfect if key is random, secret, and one-time.

flash.a: C=(p+k) mod 26; decrypt with (C−k) mod 26.
Ciphertext keeps plaintext letter-frequency patterns.
Letter pairs (digraphs) on a 5×5 square.
XOR of two ciphertexts cancels the keystream and leaks plaintext relation.

learn.concept: A transposition cipher permutes positions of plaintext symbols; the symbols themselves stay the same. Letter frequencies are unchanged, so pure transposition is easy to spot, but multiple stages (product transposition) make reconstruction harder.
learn.howItWorks:
Rail fence
- Write plaintext in a zigzag across a fixed number of rails; read off by rows.
- Key is often the rail count.

Columnar transposition
- Write plaintext into a rectangle by rows.
- Read columns in an order given by a keyword (alphabetical order of letters).
- Keyword orders columns — it is not a substitution alphabet.

Cryptanalysis cues
- Same bag of letters as plaintext → think transposition.
- Anagramming / multiple anagramming on short texts.
- Combined with substitution → classical product cipher.
learn.example: Rail fence style: plaintext “meet at the school house” written on diagonals and read by rows yields a scrambled string with the same letters. Columnar: keyword “ZEBRAS” sorts columns into a read order.
remember: Stem “same letters, different order” → transposition.
Keyword in columnar cipher orders columns — not a letter substitution.
Rail fence key ≈ number of rails.
Pure transposition keeps frequencies; digraph/position stats change.
Multiple transposition stages strengthen classical schemes.

bullets: Rail fence: zigzag write, row read.
Columnar: row write, key-ordered column read.
Frequencies of letters survive; order does not.

flash.q: What stays the same in pure transposition?
flash.a: The multiset of letters (frequencies).
Usually the number of rails (zigzag depth).
Defines the order in which columns are read.
Anagramming recovers likely plaintext order.

learn.concept: Cryptanalysis recovers plaintext and/or key by exploiting weaknesses in ciphers or their implementation. Always state the attack model: what the adversary can observe or choose. Cryptography and cryptanalysis together form cryptology — designers use attack results to harden algorithms.
learn.howItWorks:
Attack models (increasing power)
- Ciphertext-only: only Y known.
- Known-plaintext: some (X, Y) pairs known.
- Chosen-plaintext: attacker can encrypt chosen X.
- Chosen-ciphertext: attacker can decrypt chosen Y.

Methods you should name
- Brute force / exhaustive key search (needs plaintext recognition).
- Frequency analysis (monoalphabetic); Kasiski (Vigenère).
- Differential / integral ideas on block ciphers (chosen-plaintext flavour).
- Side-channel: timing, power, EM from the real device — not pure maths of the cipher.
- Dictionary, MITM on key exchange, social engineering for keys.

Design loop
- A “break” may fully recover keys or only reduce effective security below the claimed key length.
learn.example: If the stem says the analyst has matching plaintext–ciphertext pairs and wants the key, classify known-plaintext — not ciphertext-only. If they can feed chosen messages into an encryption oracle, it is chosen-plaintext.

compare.title: Known / chosen plaintext
bullets: Modern ciphers must resist these too

remember: Stem lists known pairs → known-plaintext, not ciphertext-only.
Cryptanalysis ≠ only brute force.
Exhaustive search cost scales with key-space size.
Side-channel leaks from hardware behaviour, not from the equation alone.
Security claims must name the assumed attack model.

bullets: Cryptanalysis = break or weaken ciphers without the intended key.
Classical: frequency / Kasiski; modern: differential, linear, side-channel.
Results feed back into stronger designs.

flash.a: Adversary has only ciphertext (no plaintext, no key).
Adversary can encrypt chosen plaintexts and study outputs.
Timing, power, EM, or other physical leakage of the device.
About half the key space before success (on average).

learn.concept: Steganography hides the existence of a secret payload inside innocent cover media (image, audio, video, document). Cryptography hides meaning; steganography hides presence. They are often combined: encrypt first, then embed.
learn.howItWorks:
Vocabulary
- Cover: carrier before embedding.
- Stego-object: carrier after embedding.
- Payload: the hidden data.

Common methods (SLM)
- LSB / least-significant-bit embedding in images or audio.
- Palette-based embedding in image palettes.
- Secure cover selection: pick a cover whose blocks already resemble the payload pattern.

Detection
- Steganalysis (StegExpose, hex inspection, statistical tests).
- Trade-off: capacity vs undetectability.
- Goals differ from watermarking (ownership/integrity marking vs secret messaging).
learn.example: Malware authors embed code in celebrity JPEGs or WAV files; the download looks harmless until a dropper extracts the payload. Exam cue: if the stem stresses “nobody notices a message exists,” answer steganography — not encryption alone.

compare.title: Cryptography
bullets: Hides meaning of a known message
Ciphertext is usually obvious as ciphertext

remember: Stem “hide that a message exists” → steganography.
Stem “make message unreadable” → cryptography.
LSB embedding is the classic image technique.
Detecting stego ≠ recovering a cipher’s plaintext.
Capacity vs undetectability is the usual trade-off.

bullets: Stego hides presence inside a cover.
Crypto hides meaning; often used together.
LSB / palette / cover-selection are syllabus methods.
Watermarking is related but serves a different goal.

flash.a: Innocent carrier before vs after the payload is embedded.
Replace least-significant bits of media samples with payload bits.
Crypto hides meaning; stego hides existence.
Detecting (and sometimes extracting) hidden stego payloads.

commonConfusion.title: Steganography ≠ cryptography
commonConfusion.body: **Cryptography** hides *meaning*.\n**Steganography** hides *existence* of a message inside cover media. They are often used together.

learn.concept: Stream ciphers transform plaintext one symbol/bit at a time, typically by XOR with a keystream. Block ciphers transform fixed-size blocks (e.g. 64 or 128 bits) under one key. Most modern symmetric encryption is built on block ciphers; modes (Module 2) turn blocks into message encryption.
learn.howItWorks:
Stream ciphers
- Fast, constant space; low error propagation across symbols.
- Weak diffusion: each ciphertext symbol mainly depends on one plaintext symbol.
- Keystream reuse is catastrophic (two ciphertexts XOR → plaintext relation).
- Synchronous: keystream independent of ciphertext; self-synchronising: depends on prior ciphertext.

Block ciphers
- Encrypt n-bit blocks; need padding if length is not a multiple of n.
- High diffusion inside the block; harder to insert undetected symbols.
- Slower start (need a full block); bit errors can corrupt a whole block or chained blocks.

SLM framing tip
- Simple substitution ≈ stream-like; pure transposition ≈ block-like classical analogy.
learn.example: OTP is the ideal stream idea with a truly random one-time keystream. AES-128 encrypts 128-bit chunks — that is a block cipher; AES-CTR then builds a stream-like keystream from it.

compare.title: Stream cipher
bullets: Error often local to a symbol

remember: Stem “XOR with running keystream” → stream.
Stem “encrypt 64/128-bit chunks” → block.
Never reuse a stream keystream under the same key.
ECB/CBC are modes of block ciphers, not stream ciphers themselves.
Block size choice ≠ key strength; key length drives brute-force cost.

bullets: Stream pros: speed, local errors; cons: diffusion, insertion risk, reuse.
Block pros: diffusion, tamper resistance; cons: latency, padding, block errors.
OTP is perfect stream theory; impractical at scale.
Modern practice: block cipher + mode (often stream-like CTR/GCM).

flash.a: Stream encrypts symbols continuously; block encrypts fixed-size groups.
C1⊕C2 cancels the keystream and relates the two plaintexts.
Message length must become a multiple of the block size.
DES 64-bit blocks; AES 128-bit blocks.

commonConfusion.title: Stream ≠ block
commonConfusion.body: **Stream:** continuous keystream (often XOR).\n**Block:** fixed-size chunks; modes (ECB/CBC/…) turn a block cipher into a message cipher.

learn.concept: Hardware security protects systems through physical roots of trust, isolated crypto engines, and defenses against attacks that target chips and firmware — not only the maths of an algorithm. Correct software crypto can still leak through timing, power, or EM on real silicon.
learn.howItWorks:
Roots of trust
- Immutable ROM / secure boot verifies each later stage upward.
- TPM / secure element / HSM: store keys and run crypto off the main CPU.

Threat themes in the SLM
- Hardware Trojans and supply-chain implants.
- Side-channels: power, timing, EM (Kocher-style attacks on smart cards, RSA, DSS…).
- Formal verification of security protocols’ secrecy/authentication claims.

Exam framing
- Hardware security complements algorithmic strength; it does not replace AES/RSA sizing.
- Name one concrete example (TPM, smart card, secure enclave) when asked to “define + example”.
learn.example: An AES implementation can be mathematically correct yet leak the key via differential power analysis on a smart card. Mitigations: constant-time code, masking, and keys kept inside a TPM.
remember: Stem “power analysis / timing leak” → side-channel.
Do not assume software AES is automatically safe on embedded devices.
Secure boot chains trust from hardware upward.
TPM/HSM isolate key material from the OS.
Hardware security complements — does not replace — cipher strength.

bullets: Hardware roots of trust anchor secure boot.
TPM/secure element isolate keys and crypto ops.
Side-channels attack physical leakage, not just equations.
Hardware Trojans are supply-chain / implant threats.
Always pair algorithmic crypto with implementation hardening.

flash.q: What is a hardware root of trust?
flash.a: Boot-anchored component that verifies later software stages.
Recovering a key from power traces or timing of modular exponentiation.
Dedicated chip storing keys and performing crypto in isolation.

flash.q: Does strong AES math stop side-channels?
flash.a: No — implementations can still leak on real hardware.

learn.concept: A modern block cipher is a keyed invertible map on n-bit blocks (typical n = 64 or 128). Strength comes mainly from key length and round design, not from secrecy of the algorithm. Because a huge substitution table is impossible, designers build product ciphers from smaller substitution and permutation layers repeated in rounds.
learn.howItWorks:
Principles
- Confusion + diffusion (Shannon) realised via Feistel or SPN structures.
- Rounds: repeated keyed mixing; key schedule derives round keys from the master key.
- Ideal behaviour: look like a pseudorandom permutation; avalanche (1-bit change flips ~half the bits).

Design notes from the SLM
- Block size does not by itself set strength; key length does for brute force.
- Small blocks still enable codebook / birthday issues at large volume.
- Modes of operation are separate from the primitive (next topics).

Named schemes to recognise
- DES (64-bit block, short key — legacy), 3DES, AES (Rijndael), IDEA, Twofish, Serpent.
learn.example: A 64-bit ideal cipher would need a 2^64-entry table — impossible. Instead DES/AES compose S-boxes and permutations over many rounds. Trap: calling AES a Feistel cipher — AES is SPN; DES is Feistel.

compare.title: Feistel (e.g. DES)
bullets: Split block L∥R; F on one half

remember: State block size, key size, rounds, and product-cipher idea.
Avalanche: one-bit change should scramble ciphertext unpredictably.
AES ≠ Feistel; DES = Feistel.
Mode ≠ algorithm (AES-CBC is AES in CBC mode).
Principles come before named algorithms in exam answers.

bullets: Block cipher = keyed permutation on n-bit blocks.
Built as product of substitutions/permutations over rounds.
Key schedule → round keys; avalanche is the quality check.
Feistel vs SPN are the two dominant structures.
Modes turn the primitive into message encryption.

flash.a: A full n-bit substitution table is infeasible; compose small layers instead.

flash.q: What does the key schedule do?
flash.a: Derives per-round subkeys from the master key.
Tiny plaintext/key change flips about half the ciphertext bits.
DES is Feistel; AES is an SPN (not Feistel).

2.1.2.title: Shannon’s Theory of Confusion and Diffusion

learn.concept: Claude Shannon required two properties for strong ciphers: confusion (make the ciphertext–key relation complex) and diffusion (spread plaintext statistical structure across many ciphertext bits). Either alone is insufficient; modern rounds combine nonlinear S-boxes with linear mixing.
learn.howItWorks:
Confusion
- Hide how ciphertext depends on the key.
- Primary tool: nonlinear substitution (S-boxes).
- Goal: knowing many plaintext–ciphertext pairs still should not reveal the key easily.

Diffusion
- Spread each plaintext (and key) bit’s influence across many output bits.
- Primary tool: permutation / MixColumns-style linear mixing.
- Strict avalanche: flipping bit i flips bit j with probability ~1/2.

Concrete links
- DES: S-boxes (confusion) + P-permutation (diffusion) inside Feistel rounds.
- AES: SubBytes (confusion) + ShiftRows/MixColumns (diffusion).
- SLM note: stream ciphers lean on confusion; block ciphers need both.
learn.example: Stem “hide the key–ciphertext relationship” → confusion. Stem “spread each plaintext bit’s influence” → diffusion. If asked how AES achieves them, name SubBytes vs MixColumns/ShiftRows.
remember: Confusion ↔ key complexity; diffusion ↔ spread influence.
Swapping the two definitions is the classic MCQ fail.
S-box without diffusion leaves structure; linear mixing without S-boxes is weak.
Shannon: both properties are required.
Avalanche is the practical test of good diffusion (+ confusion).

bullets: Both needed; SPNs/Feistel rounds implement them.
DES and AES map layers cleanly onto the two ideas.
Avalanche ≈ flipping one input bit flips ~half the output.

flash.a: Make ciphertext–key dependence as complex as possible.
Disperse plaintext redundancy across many ciphertext bits.
SubBytes (S-box).
ShiftRows and MixColumns.

learn.concept: The Feistel structure (Horst Feistel / Lucifer lineage) splits a block into halves L∥R and iterates keyed rounds. It is the backbone of DES and several other ciphers (Blowfish, CAST-128, KASUMI). Major engineering win: encryption and decryption share the same structure with round keys reversed.
learn.howItWorks:
Round equations
- LE_i = RE_{i−1}
- RE_i = LE_{i−1} ⊕ F(RE_{i−1}, K_i)
- F is the round function (expansion, S-boxes, permutation in DES); F need not be invertible.

Why decryption works
- XOR undoes the combine step when F’s output is recomputed from the known half and K_i.
- Run the same network with subkeys K_n … K_1.
- Final L/R swap detail matters for some variants — check the stem.

Design notes
- Number of rounds is a design parameter; weak F is not fixed by “more rounds” alone.
- Contrast SPN (AES): whole block mixed each round; inverse layers required.
learn.example: **Worked sketch:** One Feistel round swaps halves after mixing: Lᵢ₊₁ = Rᵢ and Rᵢ₊₁ = Lᵢ ⊕ F(Rᵢ, Kᵢ). Decryption uses the same round function with keys in reverse order — that is why Feistel is popular in classical DES-style designs.

compare.title: Feistel
bullets: Updates one half per round via F

remember: Write LE_i / RE_i and say decryption = reverse keys.
Stem “same algorithm for encrypt/decrypt” → Feistel property.
AES is not Feistel — do not force Feistel equations onto AES.
F needn’t be invertible because XOR undoes the combine.
Correct spelling: Feistel.

bullets: Split block; F(R, K_i) XORed into L; then swap halves.
Decrypt with reversed subkeys on the same network.

flash.a: Knowing R and K_i recomputes F; XOR recovers the other half.
Same structure with round keys in reverse order.
No — AES is an SPN.

commonConfusion.title: Feistel vs AES
commonConfusion.body: **DES** is Feistel.\n**AES** is an SPN (SubBytes / ShiftRows / MixColumns) — not Feistel.

diagram.title: Feistel round (schematic)
rows: Decrypt: same structure, reverse round keys

learn.concept: DES is a NIST-standardised 64-bit Feistel block cipher with 16 rounds. The keying material is 64 bits but only 56 bits are effective (8 parity bits). It dominated commercial crypto for decades and was superseded by AES; Triple DES remained as a transitional option.
learn.howItWorks:
Pipeline
- Initial permutation IP → split into LPT/RPT → 16 Feistel rounds → join → final permutation FP (=IP⁻¹).
- Decrypt: same algorithm, reverse the 16 subkeys.

Round f-function
- Expand R (32→48), XOR with 48-bit round key, eight 6→4 S-boxes, then P-permutation.
- S-boxes supply the main nonlinearity (confusion).

Key schedule
- PC-1, rotations, PC-2 produce sixteen 48-bit subkeys.

Properties claimed
- Avalanche and completeness: each ciphertext bit depends on many plaintext bits.
- IP/FP alone add no cryptographic strength — they are fixed permutations.
learn.example: Fingerprint stem: “56-bit key, 64-bit block, 16 rounds” → DES. Trap: saying the key is 64-bit secure — eight bits are parity only.
remember: DES: 64-bit block, 56-bit effective key, 16 Feistel rounds.
f = E + XOR K_i + S-boxes + P.
Encrypt/decrypt share structure with reversed subkeys.
IP/FP are fixed bookends — not the source of strength.
Do not confuse DES expansion with AES MixColumns.

bullets: IP → 16 rounds → FP; reverse keys to decrypt.
S-boxes are the nonlinear core of f.
Historically broken mainly by short key length (see next topic).

flash.a: 64-bit block; 56-bit effective key (64 with parity).
16 Feistel rounds.
Each S-box maps 6 bits to 4 bits (eight S-boxes).
Same algorithm with round keys K16…K1.

learn.concept: DES strength debates split into algorithm-structure concerns and the 56-bit key length. Today the practical insecurity is exhaustive search on 2^56 keys — demonstrated by specialised hardware (EFF DES cracker, 1998, under three days) — not a collapse of the Feistel idea itself.
learn.howItWorks:
Key-length issue
- ~7.2×10^16 keys; feasible for dedicated crackers and increasingly for commodity clusters.
- Longer keys (e.g. move to AES-128) defeat pure brute force.

Algorithmic concerns
- Weak / semi-weak keys with pathological schedules — avoid them.
- Complementary property used in some analyses.
- Differential and linear cryptanalysis reduce complexity vs naive brute force but remain costly for full DES.
- Oddities such as colliding S-box inputs; unclear crypto role of IP/FP.

Migration path
- 3DES extended DES hardware life; AES replaced DES for new designs.
learn.example: Stem “why is DES insecure now?” → 56-bit exhaustive search is practical. Trap: claiming “Feistel is broken” or that differential cryptanalysis “breaks DES instantly.”
remember: Main weakness today: 56-bit key space.
EFF DES cracker showed practical brute force.
Weak keys exist but are rare; examiners still love the term.
Analytical attacks ≠ instant break of full DES.
Security of DES ≠ security of a longer-key Feistel design.

bullets: Two concern classes: algorithm quirks vs 56-bit key.
DC/LC matter historically but key length dominates practice.

flash.a: 56-bit key enables exhaustive search.

flash.q: What did the 1998 EFF cracker show?
flash.a: DES can be broken by dedicated brute-force hardware in days.
Pathological keys with poor key-schedule behaviour — must be avoided.
No — short key length failed; Feistel structure remains a valid design pattern.

learn.concept: Differential cryptanalysis studies how differences between plaintext pairs propagate to ciphertext differences. Biases in those difference distributions leak information about round keys and S-boxes. It is typically a chosen-plaintext style attack using many pairs.
learn.howItWorks:
Core idea
- Choose ΔP = P ⊕ P′; encrypt both; observe ΔC = C ⊕ C′.
- A characteristic is a predicted difference path through rounds with some probability.
- Difference distribution tables summarise S-box behaviour under differentials.

Why it matters for DES/AES history
- DES S-boxes resist DC better than random boxes — design target (criteria once secret).
- Related cousin: linear cryptanalysis uses linear approximations instead of differences.

Not the same as
- Traffic analysis, side-channel power analysis, or simple known-plaintext lookup.
learn.example: Exam outline: “attacker chooses many plaintext pairs with fixed ΔP, collects ΔC statistics, matches likely characteristics, recovers key bits.” Mention probability of characteristics if asked.
remember: Stem “plaintext difference → ciphertext difference” → differential cryptanalysis.
Usually needs many chosen pairs.
Attacks nonlinear S-boxes via difference tables.
DES S-boxes were tuned against DC.
Do not confuse with side-channel or traffic analysis.

bullets: Track ΔP through rounds to biased ΔC.
S-box DDT is the analytic engine.
Linear cryptanalysis is the parallel approximation idea.

learn.concept: A block cipher encrypts one block; a mode of operation defines how to encrypt arbitrary-length messages. Mode ≠ algorithm: AES-CBC means the AES primitive used in CBC mode. Never use ECB for structured data.
learn.howItWorks:
ECB
- Independent E_K(P_i). Identical plaintext blocks → identical ciphertext (pattern leak).

CBC
- C_i = E_K(P_i ⊕ C_{i−1}); C_0 from IV. Hides repeated blocks; sequential.

CFB
- Encrypt a shift register / IV, XOR with plaintext → ciphertext fed back (self-synchronising stream-like).

OFB
- Keystream from repeatedly encrypting the register; feedback is the cipher output, not ciphertext.
- Keystream independent of plaintext.

CTR
- Encrypt nonce∥counter to make a keystream; highly parallel; never reuse counter under same key.

IV / nonce
- Uniqueness usually matters more than secrecy (mode-dependent).

Round layers

Decryption

learn.concept: Fermat’s Little Theorem and Euler’s theorem are the modular-arithmetic engines behind RSA correctness. Fermat is the prime-modulus special case of Euler. You will use φ(n) when choosing decryption exponents.
learn.howItWorks:
Fermat’s Little Theorem
- If p is prime and gcd(a,p)=1, then a^(p−1) ≡ 1 (mod p).
- Alternate form: a^p ≡ a (mod p) for prime p.

Euler’s totient φ(n)
- Count of integers in 1..n−1 coprime to n; φ(1)=1.
- If p prime: φ(p)=p−1.
- If n=pq distinct primes: φ(n)=(p−1)(q−1).

Euler’s theorem
- If gcd(a,n)=1, then a^φ(n) ≡ 1 (mod n).

RSA link
- Choose e with gcd(e, φ(n))=1; d ≡ e⁻¹ (mod φ(n)) so ed ≡ 1 (mod φ(n)).
- Then M^(ed) ≡ M (mod n) under standard conditions.

learn.concept: The Chinese Remainder Theorem (CRT) says a system x ≡ a_i (mod m_i) has a unique solution modulo M = ∏ m_i when the moduli are pairwise coprime. It is both an exam calculation tool and the standard speedup for RSA decryption (compute mod p and mod q, then combine).

1. M = m1 m2 … mn.

4. x = (∑ a_i Z_i M_i) mod M.

learn.concept: Public-key (asymmetric) cryptography uses a related key pair: a public key anyone may use to encrypt or verify, and a private key kept secret for decrypt or sign. Security rests on trapdoor one-way functions (factoring, discrete log), not on hiding the public key.
learn.howItWorks:
Core principles (SLM list condensed)
- Key pairs: public ↔ private mathematically linked; private not feasibly derived from public.
- Confidentiality: encrypt with recipient’s public key; only their private key decrypts.
- Signatures: sign with sender’s private key; verify with sender’s public key.
- Authentication / challenge-response using private-key proofs.
- Key exchange (e.g. Diffie–Hellman) builds shared secrets over open channels.

Practice
- Public-key ops are slow → hybrid encryption: wrap an AES session key with RSA/ECC, bulk-encrypt with AES.
- Trust in public keys needs PKI or web-of-trust (later modules).

learn.concept: RSA (Rivest–Shamir–Adleman) is the classic public-key cryptosystem based on modular exponentiation and the hardness of factoring n = pq. Public key (n, e); private exponent d (and usually p, q). Correctness follows from Euler/Fermat once ed ≡ 1 (mod φ(n)).
learn.howItWorks:
Key generation
1. Choose large secret primes p, q; n = pq.
2. φ(n) = (p−1)(q−1).
3. Pick e with gcd(e, φ(n))=1 (often 65537).
4. d ≡ e⁻¹ (mod φ(n)).
5. Publish (n, e); keep d (and p, q) private.

Encrypt / decrypt
- C = M^e mod n (0 < M < n, with padding in practice).
- M = C^d mod n.

Signing variant
- Sign with d; verify with e — same maths, authenticity goal.

Practice warning
- Textbook/raw RSA is malleable; use padding (OAEP, etc.).

learn.concept: RSA security, under good parameters, rests on the hardness of factoring n (and related RSA problems). If p and q are known, φ(n) and d follow and the scheme collapses. In practice, bad parameters and bad implementations fail long before asymptotic factoring breakthroughs.

- Use large keys (historically 1024 → 2048+ bits) and vetted libraries.

- Quantum note: Shor’s algorithm threatens factoring/DL schemes — RSA is not quantum-safe.

learn.concept: Message authentication checks that a received message really came from the claimed sender and was not altered in transit. A MAC is a short cryptographic tag built from the message and a shared secret key; only parties who know that key can produce a matching tag. Encryption alone does not always give authenticity, and a MAC alone does not hide message content — the two goals are separate.
learn.howItWorks:
Key vocabulary:
- **Message authentication** — Verify claimed origin and detect alteration.
- **MAC (idea)** — Short authentication tag computed with a shared secret key.
- **Impersonation / alteration** — Active threats authentication aims to catch.
- **Secrecy vs authenticity** — Encryption ≠ authentication; MAC ≠ confidentiality.

How the pieces fit:
- Sender computes tag = MAC_K(M) and sends M with the tag (M may be clear or encrypted).
- Receiver recomputes the tag with the same K and compares.
- Replay can still succeed unless freshness (nonce/timestamp) is added.
- Digital signatures are the asymmetric counterpart when third-party proof is needed.

learn.concept: Authentication sits on two layers: a lower function that produces an authenticator value, then a protocol that uses that value to accept or reject a message. Textbooks group the lower functions into three classical classes — message encryption, message authentication codes, and hash-function schemes. Choosing the class decides whether a secret key is needed and what an attacker who can rewrite the message can forge.

Key vocabulary:
- **Authentication function** — Produces an authenticator from the message (±key).

- **Hash authenticator** — Unkeyed fixed-length digest; needs binding (encrypt digest, HMAC, or sign).

- Encryption path needs recognisable plaintext structure (e.g. FCS) or it is ambiguous.
- Hash alone is public — attacker can recompute digest after modification.
- MAC binds K so forging tags without K is computationally hard.

learn.concept: Network messaging faces a catalogue of threats: disclosure, traffic analysis, masquerade, content change, sequence change, timing/replay, and source or destination repudiation. Message secrecy counters disclosure and traffic analysis; message authentication counters masquerade through timing attacks; digital signatures (often with extra protocol) handle repudiation. MAC requirements therefore centre on integrity and origin among parties who share a key — not confidentiality, and not court-grade non-repudiation.
learn.howItWorks:
Key vocabulary:
- **Disclosure / traffic analysis** — Secrecy concerns, not MAC goals.
- **Content integrity** — Detect modification of message bits.
- **Origin authentication** — Assure claimed sender really sent it.
- **Sequencing / timeliness** — Detect replay, reordering, delay when required.
- **Non-repudiation** — Usually needs signatures/TTP — not ordinary MAC.

How the pieces fit:
- Requirements track the threat model: integrity alone vs integrity+freshness.
- Same valid MAC can be resent — add nonce/timestamp when replay matters.
- Encryption requirements are separate; mix only when the stem asks for both.

learn.concept: A MAC algorithm takes a message and a shared key and outputs a fixed-length tag. The receiver recomputes the tag and accepts only on equality. learn.concept: SHA is the NIST family of iterative one-way hash functions that map arbitrary-length input to a fixed-length digest. Digests support integrity checks, HMAC, digital signatures, and fingerprinting. Cryptographic hashes aim for preimage, second-preimage, and collision resistance; SHA-1’s 160-bit digest is collision-broken for practical attacks, while SHA-2 (e.g. SHA-256) and SHA-3 (sponge/Keccak) are the modern choices.

- **SHA family** — SHA-1 (legacy); SHA-2 (224/256/384/512); SHA-3 variants.

- **SHA-256** — Common SHA-2 workhorse with 256-bit digest.
- **One-way / compression** — Fixed output via iterated compression (SHA-2) or sponge (SHA-3).

How the pieces fit:
- Preprocess (pad, block) then iterate compression to a final digest.
- Longer digests raise birthday-bound collision cost.
- Hash ≠ encryption: not secret-key reversible transforms.
- Used inside HMAC and hash-then-sign pipelines.

- Digest length is not confidentiality strength.

learn.concept: A digital signature is an asymmetric authenticator that binds a message to a signer’s private key. Anyone with the matching public key can verify; no shared secret is required. Signatures deliver integrity, origin authentication, and non-repudiation (assuming the private key was not compromised). They do not hide content unless combined with encryption. Practice almost always hashes first, then signs the digest.
learn.howItWorks:
Key vocabulary:
- **Digital signature** — Asymmetric binding of message to private key.
- **Sign / Verify** — Sign with private key; verify with public key.
- **Non-repudiation** — Signer cannot credibly deny the signature if key was secure.
- **Hash-then-sign** — Hash message; sign the digest for efficiency.

How the pieces fit:
- Message and signature travel together; verifier recomputes digest and runs verify.
- Unlike handwritten signatures, verification is algorithmic, not visual matching.
- Key compromise and revocation affect trust in past and future signatures.
learn.example: Alice signs a contract digest with her private key; Bob and a court verify with Alice’s public key. Exam habit: “private key creates, public key checks” → signature; encrypting with the public key is not signing.

bullets: Shared secret for create and verify

commonConfusion.body: **Sign** with the private key; **verify** with the public key.\nSignatures prove origin/integrity/non-repudiation — they are not bulk confidentiality.

learn.concept: DSS is NIST’s Digital Signature Standard (FIPS) that specifies approved algorithms for creating digital signatures, typically using SHA digests. DSA — the classic DSS algorithm — signs using discrete-log hardness in a subgroup with global parameters (p, q, g) and a per-user key pair. Later DSS revisions may also allow RSA signatures and ECDSA. Classical DSA is signature-only: it does not encrypt files.
learn.howItWorks:
Key vocabulary:
- **DSS** — NIST framework for approved signature algorithms.
- **DSA** — Discrete-log subgroup signature algorithm under DSS.
- **Parameters** — Domain (p,q,g) plus user key pair (x private, y=g^x public).
- **Per-message k** — Fresh secret randomness; reuse is catastrophic.

How the pieces fit:
- DSS = standard; DSA = specific algorithm often tested under DSS.
- Hash strength is part of overall signature security.
- Verifier needs public key and (for DSA/ECDSA) domain parameters.
learn.example: Exam stem “NIST signature standard” → DSS; “discrete log subgroup signature” → DSA. Habit: never say DSS encrypts documents — it standardises signatures.

compare.title: DSS / DSA
bullets: Needs unique secret nonce k per signature

compare.title: RSA signatures
bullets: Often allowed under broader DSS revisions
Same key pair family can also encrypt (different use)

remember: Stem “NIST signature standard” → DSS.
Stem “discrete log subgroup signature” → DSA.
Trap: saying DSS encrypts files.
Random nonce k must be unique and secret per signature.
DSS uses SHA for the message digest being signed.

bullets: DSS is the NIST FIPS signature standard framework.
DSA is the classic DSS discrete-log algorithm.

Digital Signature Algorithm based on discrete log in a subgroup.

learn.concept: DSA correctness shows that an honest signature (r, s) built with private x and hash H(M) will satisfy the verification equation that reconstructs r using public y = g^x. Altered messages change H(M) and fail verification with overwhelming probability. Security rests on discrete-log hardness and on keeping both x and the per-message nonce k secret. Exam “prove DSA works” questions expect the verify-equals-r algebra, not an RSA proof.
learn.howItWorks:
Key vocabulary:
- **DSA signing (schematic)** — r from g^k mod p; s from k⁻¹(H(M)+x·r) mod q.
- **DSA verify** — Recompute using public y and check reconstructed value matches r.
- **Correctness** — Verify accepts iff signature came from x and H(M).
- **Security basis** — Hardness of discrete logarithm in the chosen group.

How the pieces fit:
- Private x never leaves the signer; y is published.
- Hash function strength is part of signature security.
- If k leaks or repeats, x can be recovered — implementation obligation.
learn.example: Worked habit: write sign steps → write verify steps → show substitution yields r when H(M) and (r,s) are honest. Trap to avoid: pasting RSA’s ed ≡ 1 mod φ(n) proof into a DSA question.
remember: Stem “prove/show DSA works” → expand verify equals r using algebra mod q.
Trap: omitting the hash H(M) in the equations.
If k leaks or repeats, private x can be recovered.
Don’t paste RSA proof when the question is DSA.
Public y = g^x; private x stays with the signer.

bullets: Honest DSA signatures satisfy the verify equation for r.
Altered M changes H(M) and fails verification.
Security = discrete log + secret x and k.
k reuse is a catastrophic implementation failure.

flash.a: Verify accepts honest signatures and rejects altered M with high probability.

flash.a: The private key x can be recovered.

learn.concept: Kerberos is a trusted-third-party authentication protocol for open networks. A Key Distribution Center (AS + TGS) issues tickets using symmetric cryptography so users authenticate once and obtain service tickets without repeatedly sending passwords to every server. Classic teaching Kerberos is not a public-key PKI system. Timestamps in authenticators assume loosely synchronised clocks.
learn.howItWorks:
Key vocabulary:
- **Kerberos** — Ticket-based authentication with a trusted KDC.
- **KDC** — Authentication Server (AS) + Ticket Granting Server (TGS).
- **TGT** — Ticket-Granting Ticket proving AS authentication to get service tickets.
- **Service ticket** — Credential presented to an application server.
- **Authenticator** — Fresh encrypted timestamp proving session-key possession (anti-replay).

How the pieces fit:
- Client → AS → TGT → TGS → service ticket → app server verifies.
- Passwords typically protect the AS exchange; long-term keys stay with KDC/servers.
- Mutual authentication is optional; Kerberos does not by itself encrypt all app data.
learn.example: **Ticket walk-through:** Client authenticates to the AS and receives a TGT. With the TGT, the client asks the TGS for a service ticket. The service ticket is then presented to the application server — the server never sees the password.

compare.title: Kerberos
bullets: SSO/authn inside a realm via tickets
Classic design uses symmetric crypto + KDC

compare.title: SSL/TLS
bullets: Secures a transport session (often with certificates)

Protects data on the wire to a server

Trap: calling Kerberos a public-key PKI system.

learn.concept: An Access Control List attaches to an object and lists which subjects may perform which operations. Authentication identifies who you are; the ACL authorises what you may do afterward. ACLs are the object-centric view of an access matrix; capability lists are the subject-centric dual. Owner-managed ACLs are a common discretionary access control realisation. Network ACLs that filter traffic by address/port are a related but distinct use of the same “list of allowed actions” idea.
learn.howItWorks:
Key vocabulary:
- **ACL** — Per-object list of subjects and permitted rights.
- **Subject / Object** — Active entity (user/process) / passive resource.
- **Access right** — read, write, execute, delete, etc.
- **Capability** — Unforgeable token held by a subject naming allowed operations.

How the pieces fit:
- Access matrix column ≈ ACL; row ≈ capability list.
- ACLs scale per resource; enumerating “everything user X can access” can be costly.
- Default-deny vs default-allow changes posture sharply.
learn.example: File report.docx ACL: Alice r/w, Bob r, others none. Exam habit: “permissions on the file listing users” → ACL; “token carried by process” → capability. Don’t confuse Kerberos authentication with ACL authorisation.

bullets: Natural “who may touch this file?” query

compare.title: Capability
bullets: Natural “what can this process do?” query

Stem “permissions on the file listing users” → ACL.
Stem “token carried by process” → capability, not ACL.
Trap: mixing authentication (Kerberos) with authorisation (ACL).
Access matrix: column = ACL; row = capability list.

4.1.3.title: Electronic Mail Security: Pretty Good Privacy (PGP)

learn.concept: Pretty Good Privacy secures email and files with hybrid cryptography: a random symmetric session key encrypts the bulk message; public-key crypto wraps that session key for the recipient. Signatures hash the message and sign with the sender’s private key. Trust is often a decentralised web of trust (users sign keys) rather than a single corporate CA hierarchy — the classic contrast with S/MIME.
learn.howItWorks:
Key vocabulary:
- **PGP** — Hybrid encrypt + sign for email/files.
- **Web of trust** — Decentralised key endorsement by users.
- **Session key** — Symmetric key for bulk; RSA/ElGamal wraps it.
- **Key rings** — Local public/private keys and trust metadata.

How the pieces fit:
- Compression often precedes encryption in the PGP pipeline.
- Private key decrypts the session key, not each message byte.
- Revocation and key authenticity remain user-managed problems.
learn.example: Alice encrypts a report to Bob: generate session key → encrypt message → encrypt session key with Bob’s public key → optionally sign. Exam habit: “friends sign keys / no central CA required” → PGP; do not claim RSA encrypts the entire body.
remember: hybrid encryption + web of trust are the PGP headlines.
Stem “friends sign keys / no central CA required” → PGP.
Trap: saying PGP only uses RSA on the whole email body.
Private key unwraps the session key.
Contrast with S/MIME: corporate PKI vs web of trust.

bullets: PGP = hybrid bulk encrypt + public-key wrap + optional sign.
Web of trust is decentralised key trust.
Session key encrypts content; asymmetric wraps the key.
Not the same trust model as S/MIME X.509.

flash.a: Pretty Good Privacy — hybrid encryption and signing for email/files.

flash.q: What is the web of trust?
flash.a: Users sign others’ keys; trust is decentralised, not only CA-based.

flash.q: How does PGP encrypt bulk mail?
flash.a: Symmetric session key encrypts the message; public key wraps that session key.

learn.concept: S/MIME (Secure/Multipurpose Internet Mail Extensions) adds encryption and digital signatures to MIME email using asymmetric cryptography and X.509 certificates. Both sides typically need S/MIME enabled and valid certificates bound to their addresses. The crypto idea mirrors PGP’s hybrid model, but trust follows enterprise CA hierarchies, CRLs/OCSP, and certificate validation — not a casual web of trust.
learn.howItWorks:
Key vocabulary:
- **S/MIME** — MIME + PKI-based mail security.
- **X.509 certificates** — CA-issued identity↔public-key bindings.
- **Enveloped data** — Encrypted content for confidentiality.
- **Signed data** — Cryptographic signature over MIME entities.

How the pieces fit:
- Encrypt with recipient public key material; decrypt with recipient private key.
- Sign with sender private key; verify with sender public key / certificate.
- S/MIME ≠ SSL: end-to-end mail vs transport session to a server.
learn.example: Corporate Outlook: padlock/signature icons show enveloped and signed mail when certificates are enrolled. Exam habit: “MIME security with X.509 / CA” → S/MIME; “corporate CA” is not web-of-trust PGP.

compare.title: SSL/TLS
bullets: Protects hop to mail server, not necessarily end-to-end body crypto
Different layer than S/MIME message security

Trap: web of trust answer when the stem says corporate CA.
S/MIME ≠ SSL.

learn.concept: IPsec is a network-layer security architecture for IP traffic, which has no native confidentiality or authenticity. Core pieces include Authentication Header (AH), Encapsulating Security Payload (ESP), Security Associations / Security Policy Databases, and key management (IKE/IKEv2). Transport mode protects upper-layer payload; tunnel mode encapsulates whole IP packets and is common for VPNs between gateways.
learn.howItWorks:
Key vocabulary:
- **IPsec** — IP-layer security framework.
- **AH** — Integrity/authenticity of IP packet parts — no encryption.
- **ESP** — Confidentiality ± integrity for payload.
- **SA / SPD** — Negotiated crypto params / policy of what to protect.
- **Transport vs tunnel** — Payload protection vs whole-packet encapsulation.

How the pieces fit:
- SPD decides; SA describes the live negotiated connection.
- Anti-replay uses sequence numbers.
- Operates below many apps — transparent compared with PGP.
learn.example: Site-to-site VPN: gateways use IPsec tunnel mode with ESP so branch traffic is encrypted across the Internet. Exam habit: AH = integrity-only; ESP can encrypt; don’t place IPsec at the application layer like PGP.

compare.title: AH
bullets: Protects selected IP header fields + payload

remember: Stem “AH vs ESP” → integrity-only vs encrypting payload.
Tunnel mode common for gateway VPNs.
Trap: placing IPsec at the application layer like PGP.
SPD decides; SA describes negotiated connection.
IKE negotiates keys and SAs.

bullets: IPsec secures IP at the network layer.
SA/SPD + IKE manage policy and keys.

flash.a: Security architecture for IP — AH, ESP, and key management.
AH provides integrity/auth without encryption; ESP can encrypt the payload.
Transport protects upper payload; tunnel encapsulates whole IP packets.
Security Association — the negotiated cryptographic parameters for a connection.

learn.concept: SSL (and its successor TLS) provides confidentiality, integrity, and authentication for a transport-layer session — the technology behind HTTPS padlocks. A handshake negotiates version and ciphers, authenticates the server (usually via X.509 certificate), and derives session keys; the record protocol then protects application data. SSL/TLS secures the hop to the server; it is not end-to-end email crypto like PGP/S/MIME.
learn.howItWorks:
Key vocabulary:
- **SSL/TLS** — Secure transport protocol (TLS is the modern name).
- **Handshake** — Negotiate ciphers, authenticate, derive keys.
- **Record protocol** — Fragment, MAC/AEAD, encrypt application data.
- **Certificates** — Bind server (optional client) names to public keys.

How the pieces fit:
- Cipher suites select key exchange, bulk cipher, and MAC/AEAD.
- Handshake failure ≠ record-layer bug — different subprotocols.
- IPsec vs SSL: IP layer vs above-TCP deployment.
learn.example: Browser connects to bank.com: validates certificate, finishes TLS handshake, then sends HTTP inside the encrypted record layer. Exam habit: “browser padlock / HTTPS” → SSL/TLS; don’t equate with PGP end-to-end mail.

compare.title: SSL/TLS
bullets: Protects data to the server endpoint

compare.title: IPsec
bullets: Often gateway VPN transparent to apps

remember: Stem “browser padlock / HTTPS” → SSL/TLS.
Trap: equating SSL with end-to-end mail crypto.
Handshake ≠ record protocol.
TLS is the standardised successor; exams often say SSL loosely.
IPsec vs SSL: IP layer vs transport session.

bullets: Handshake sets up keys; record protects data.
Not a substitute for PGP/S/MIME end-to-end mail.

flash.a: Confidentiality, integrity, and authentication for a transport session.
Negotiate version/ciphers, authenticate (usually server cert), derive session keys.
Protects application data (MAC/AEAD + encryption) after the handshake.
Transport to a server vs end-to-end mail/file crypto.

learn.concept: Secure Electronic Transaction is an application-level payment-card protocol designed so cardholder, merchant, and bank/payment gateway can authenticate each other while protecting payment data. Its signature idea is the dual signature: order details are bound for the merchant and payment details for the bank without fully cross-revealing both. SET is a classic exam topic; modern web checkout often uses TLS plus tokenisation instead.
learn.howItWorks:
Key vocabulary:
- **SET** — Card purchase protocol with dual signatures and certificates.
- **Dual signature** — Links order info and payment info without full cross-disclosure.
- **Payment gateway** — Interface between merchant and issuer/acquirer networks.
- **Certificates** — Cardholder, merchant, and bank/gateway roles in SET PKI.

How the pieces fit:
- Aims: authenticate parties, protect payment data, integrity, privacy split merchant/bank.
- Merchant need not see full payment credentials; bank need not see full order details.
- Not a general VPN and not “just SSL on a shop site.”

Links order info for merchant and payment info for bank without cross-revealing both.

SET is payment-application security with dual signatures; SSL is transport session encryption.
SET.

learn.concept: An intrusion is an unauthorised act of using, misusing, or attempting to misuse a system — broader than “virus.” Classic intruder classes are masquerader (outsider pretending to be legitimate), misfeasor (insider exceeding authority), and clandestine user (seizing control to evade auditing). Attacks often progress through reconnaissance, initial access, privilege escalation, lateral movement, and collection/exfiltration. Prevention, detection, and recovery are complementary controls.
learn.howItWorks:
Key vocabulary:
- **Intrusion** — Unauthorised use/misuse attempt against a system.
- **Masquerader** — Outsider impersonating a legitimate user.
- **Misfeasor** — Insider who abuses authorised access.
- **Clandestine user** — Seizes supervisory control to hide activity.
- **Audit trail** — Logs supporting detection and forensics.

How the pieces fit:
- SLM phases emphasise inspection/recon → exploitation → digging deeper → finding targets → collect/exploit.
- Insider misfeasors already have credentials — different detection profile than outsiders.
- Links forward to IDS techniques as the detection response.
learn.example: Phishing gives an outsider a password (masquerader). An employee dumps a customer DB they may read but not export (misfeasor). Exam habit: define intrusion + name the three intruder classes.

bullets: Often needs stolen credentials or exploits

compare.title: Misfeasor

Stem “outsider pretends to be legitimate” → masquerader.

Clandestine user seizes supervisory control to evade auditing.

bullets: Typical stages from recon to exfiltration.

learn.concept: An Intrusion Detection System monitors hosts or networks for suspicious activity and alerts (or feeds a SIEM). Placement and method matter: HIDS watches a host’s logs/files/processes; NIDS watches segment traffic; protocol/application-protocol and hybrid designs also appear in the SLM. Signature detection matches known patterns; anomaly detection flags deviations from a baseline. Detection is not prevention — an IPS actively blocks.

Key vocabulary:
- **IDS** — Monitors and alerts on suspicious activity.
- **HIDS** — Host logs, files, processes.
- **NIDS** — Packets/traffic on a segment.
- **Signature detection** — Known attack patterns.
- **Anomaly detection** — Deviation from normal behaviour.

How the pieces fit:
- Tuning trades false positives vs false negatives.
- NIDS may miss encrypted payload details; HIDS sees host outcomes.
- Hybrid deployments combine sensors and methods.
- PIDS/APIDS watch protocol streams (e.g. HTTPS front-end, SQL to DB).

IDS detects/alerts; IPS can actively block.

learn.concept: A virus attaches to a host program or file and spreads when that host runs or is shared. A worm is standalone malware that self-replicates across networks without needing a host file. A Trojan disguises itself as legitimate software and classically does not self-replicate. Payloads may erase data, spy, open backdoors, or run ransomware. Not all malware is a “virus.”
learn.howItWorks:
Key vocabulary:
- **Virus** — Needs a host file/program to attach and execute.
- **Worm** — Autonomous network self-propagation.
- **Trojan** — Deceptive program; not classic self-replicator.
- **Payload** — Damaging/spying action after infection.
- **Vectors** — Email, media, network services, drive-by downloads.

How the pieces fit:
- Polymorphic/metamorphic viruses change code to evade signatures.
- Macro viruses in documents are still viruses by the attachment model.
- Prevention: patching, least privilege, filtering, awareness, plus AV/EDR.

learn.concept: A firewall is a policy enforcement point that controls traffic between networks, typically at a perimeter. Designs range from packet filters (header fields such as IP/port/protocol) through stateful inspection (connection tracking) to application proxies/gateways that understand protocols in depth. A DMZ holds public services in a screened subnet apart from the internal LAN. Firewalls are choke-point controls — they do not replace patching, authentication, or encryption.

Key vocabulary:
- **Firewall** — Allow/deny traffic per policy between zones.
- **Packet filter** — Stateless or simple header rules.
- **Stateful inspection** — Tracks connection state.
- **Application proxy** — Intermediates app protocols; deeper policy.
- **DMZ** — Screened subnet for public-facing hosts.

How the pieces fit:
- Default-deny is safer than default-allow.
- Egress filtering limits exfiltration and botnet callbacks.
- Insiders with USB malware bypass perimeter firewalls.

5.1.5.title: Global Standards IT Acts and Cyber Laws

learn.concept: Cyber laws define offences, penalties, and rules for electronic records and intermediaries; technical controls implement compliance. In Indian exam contexts this often means the IT Act 2000 and its amendments covering unauthorised access, data theft, fraud, and related crimes. Digital evidence must meet authenticity procedures to be admissible. Jurisdiction and attribution are hard — logs and forensics matter in prosecution. Global flavours include unauthorised-access statutes and privacy regimes depending on syllabus focus.
learn.howItWorks:
Key vocabulary:
- **IT Act (India context)** — Legal framework for cyber offences and electronic records.
- **Cyber crime categories** — Unauthorised access, theft, fraud, identity offences, etc.
- **Electronic evidence** — Digital records with procedural authenticity requirements.
- **Compliance duties** — Reasonable security practices / privacy safeguards under rules.

How the pieces fit:
- Law sets duties and offences; firewalls and crypto are technical means.
- Amendments expanded coverage after the early Act.
- Overlaps privacy/piracy topics but is not identical to them.
learn.example: Company reports a breach: investigators preserve logs under chain-of-custody so charges under the IT Act can use admissible evidence. Exam habit: “legal act for cyber offences in India” → IT Act family — not “install a firewall” alone.

5.1.7.title: Recent Network Attacks and Security Measures

learn.concept: Modern network attacks include DDoS floods, phishing/social engineering, ransomware extortion, and long-running APTs. Real incidents in study material underline isolation, investigation, and vigilance against phishing. Defences combine prevention (patching, MFA, segmentation, filtering), detection (threat intel, monitoring), and resilience (backups, incident response). Technical crypto does not stop a user who is tricked into giving credentials.

- **Mitigations** — Patch, MFA, segment, backup, filter, least privilege.

learn.concept: A blockchain is an append-only distributed ledger of hashed, chained blocks agreed by a consensus protocol. Each block links to the previous hash so tampering is detectable; rewriting history requires redosing consensus work or controlling enough validators. Strengths are integrity and transparency; confidentiality and key custody are not automatic. Public and permissioned ledgers differ on who may validate.

- **Block** — Transactions plus link to previous hash.
- **Consensus** — PoW/PoS/etc. agreement on next state.
- **Immutability (practical)** — Costly to alter confirmed history.
- **Smart contract** — Programmable on-chain logic (platform-dependent).

How the pieces fit:
- Hash chaining detects tampering; consensus resists easy attacker forks.
- Lost private keys ⇒ lost assets.
- Not a drop-in access-control replacement inside enterprise apps.

learn.concept: Internet privacy is about controlling collection, use, and disclosure of personal data online (PII, tracking cookies, profiling). The topics share policy space but different aims: personal-data rights versus intellectual-property enforcement. Encryption helps privacy but does not erase metadata leakage.

- **Tracking / cookies** — Common profiling privacy threats.

- Privacy aids: HTTPS, minimisation, consent, anonymisation.
- Anti-piracy aids: DRM, watermarking, legal process.
- IT/IP law backs both; tech enforces imperfectly.

learn.concept: Cyber forensics is the disciplined collection, preservation, analysis, and presentation of digital evidence so events can be reconstructed for investigation or court. Methodology and legal admissibility matter more than ad-hoc browsing of a suspect machine. Volatile evidence (RAM, network state) and non-volatile media need different acquisition priorities. Chain of custody documents handling so evidence integrity can be defended; hashing verifies images were not altered.
learn.howItWorks:
Key vocabulary:

- **Goal** — Reconstruct events while keeping evidential integrity.

- **Chain of custody** — Documented handling history.

How the pieces fit:
- Differs from pure incident-response containment, though they interact.
- Never modify the live suspect disk as your first step — image first.
- Overview before detailed process (5.2.2) and tools (5.2.4).

learn.concept: Forensic work follows a standard pipeline: identify evidence sources and scope; preserve (isolate, write-block, prevent change); collect/acquire bit-for-bit images; examine/analyse artefacts and timelines; present findings clearly. Documentation runs continuously, not only at the final report. Order of volatility guides live systems. Analysis must be reproducible from the verified forensic image.

Key vocabulary:
- **Identification** — Recognise sources and scope.
- **Preservation** — Isolate, image, write-block.
- **Collection / acquisition** — Bit-for-bit imaging and labelling.
- **Examination / analysis** — Recover artefacts, deleted data, logs, timelines.
- **Presentation** — Report for investigators/court.

How the pieces fit:
- Write blockers and hash verification protect preservation claims.
- Never analyse the original read/write instead of a verified image.
- Weak custody docs undermine even strong technical findings.

learn.concept: Forensic tools cover imaging (dd-family, FTK Imager-class), analysis suites (EnCase, Autopsy/Sleuth Kit-class), write blockers, hashing utilities, memory capture/analysis, and network captures (Wireshark-class). - **Memory tools** — Capture/analyse RAM.

- Network PCAP complements host forensics.

learn.concept: Digital evidence is information of probative value stored or transmitted in digital form — active files, logs, deleted/slack space, and metadata. Contact leaves traces (digital Locard): timestamps, authors, EXIF, filesystem attributes. Integrity is protected by imaging, hashing, custody, and controlled analysis of working copies. Metadata can be forged, so corroborate across artefacts. Admissibility needs relevance, authenticity, and lawful collection.

- Original vs working copy: analyse copies; preserve originals.
- Timestamps need timezone and clock-skew interpretation.
- Screenshots alone are weak without raw sources.

learn.concept: OS-specific artefact maps drive investigations. Live response uses known-good tools before power-down decisions; rootkits can undermine live trust.

learn.concept: Email tracing reconstructs a message’s path by analysing Received headers and related metadata, then corroborating with MTA and gateway logs. The visible From: address is easily spoofed; server-added Received chains are more trustworthy but still need care. Headers are usually read bottom-up toward the originating hop. Tracing builds attribution hypotheses — it is forensic reconstruction of delivery, not PGP cryptography.

- Timezones and relay delays matter for timelines.
- Different goal than decrypting PGP mail.
